claim: Malfunction of the CFTR protein results in cystic fibrosis, one of the most common hereditary diseases.
source: Malfunction of the CFTR protein results in cystic fibrosis, one of the most common hereditary diseases.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CFTR and cystic fibrosis, widely accepted in the medical and scientific community.

claim: CFTR functions as an anion channel, the gating of which is controlled by long-range allosteric communications.
source: CFTR functions as an anion channel, the gating of which is controlled by long-range allosteric communications.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR function supported by prior research in the field.

claim: The most effective CFTR drugs modulate its activity allosterically.
source: the most effective CFTR drugs modulate its activity allosterically
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about CFTR drug mechanisms and is referenced in the context of the study.

claim: The study integrated Gaussian network model, transfer entropy, and anisotropic normal mode-Langevin dynamics to investigate the allosteric communications network of CFTR.
source: we integrated Gaussian network model, transfer entropy, and anisotropic normal mode-Langevin dynamics and investigated the allosteric communications network of CFTR
evidence: This describes the computational methods used in the study as stated in the abstract and detailed in the methods section.

claim: The computational results are in remarkable agreement with experimental observations and mutational analysis.
source: The results are in remarkable agreement with experimental observations and mutational analysis
evidence: This claim is supported by comparisons made throughout the manuscript between computational predictions and experimental data, including statistical analyses shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Residues that serve as pivotal allosteric sources and transducers were identified, many of which correspond to disease-causing mutations.
source: We identified residues that serve as pivotal allosteric sources and transducers, many of which correspond to disease-causing mutations.
evidence: This is supported by the GNM-TE analysis and statistical validation comparing identified residues with known disease-causing mutations from the cftr2 database.

claim: In the ATP-free form, dynamic fluctuations of the residues that comprise the ATP-binding sites facilitate the initial binding of the nucleotide.
source: We find that in the ATP-free form, dynamic fluctuations of the residues that comprise the ATP-binding sites facilitate the initial binding of the nucleotide.
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE analysis showing that allosteric peaks are located near ATP-binding sites even in the ATP-free state.

claim: Binding of ATP brings to the fore and focuses on dynamic fluctuations that were present in a latent and diffuse form in the absence of ATP.
source: Subsequent binding of ATP then brings to the fore and focuses on dynamic fluctuations that were present in a latent and diffuse form in the absence of ATP.
evidence: This is supported by comparing GNM-TE results between ATP-free and ATP-bound states, showing that ATP binding focuses diffuse dynamics to specific locations.

claim: Drugs that potentiate CFTR's conductance do so not by directly acting on the gating residues, but rather by mimicking the allosteric signal sent by the ATP-binding sites.
source: We demonstrate that drugs that potentiate CFTR's conductance do so not by directly acting on the gating residues, but rather by mimicking the allosteric signal sent by the ATP-binding sites.
evidence: This is supported by GNM-TE analysis showing that ivacaftor binding site sends information to similar residues as ATP-binding sites (Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.83).

claim: A previously undiscovered allosteric 'hotspot' was uncovered located proximal to the docking site of the phosphorylated regulatory (R) domain.
source: We have also uncovered a previously undiscovered allosteric 'hotspot' located proximal to the docking site of the phosphorylated regulatory (R) domain
evidence: This is identified through GNM-TE analysis after removing the slowest modes, revealing a cluster of residues in TMD1 near the R domain docking site.

claim: Cystic fibrosis affects approximately 1 in every 3000 newborns.
source: affecting approximately 1 in every 3000 newborns (Farrell, 2008)
evidence: This is cited from Farrell, 2008.

claim: Most CF patients carry a deletion of Phe 508 in nucleotide binding domain (NBD)1 which leads to protein instability and premature degradation.
source: Most CF patients carry a deletion of Phe 508 in nucleotide binding domain (NBD)1 which leads to protein instability and premature degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the most common CF mutation.

claim: More than 2000 disease-associated mutations have been documented in CFTR.
source: More than 2000 other disease-associated mutations have been documented (Cftr2.org, 2011)
evidence: This is cited from the Cftr2.org database, 2011.

claim: CFTR functions as a chloride channel, the excretion of which is important for mucus hydration.
source: CFTR functions as a chloride channel, the excretion of which is important for mucus hydration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR function.

claim: Malfunction of CFTR leads to mucus dehydration and a subsequent decrease in mucus clearance.
source: Malfunction of CFTR leads to mucus dehydration and a subsequent decrease in mucus clearance.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CF pathophysiology, supported by citation to Fahy and Dickey, 2010.

claim: CFTR is a member of the ABC transporter protein family.
source: CFTR is a member of the ABC transporter protein family
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR classification.

claim: ABC transporter family is considered to be one of the largest protein families of any proteome.
source: considered to be one of the largest protein families of any proteome (Dean et al., 2001)
evidence: This is cited from Dean et al., 2001.

claim: CFTR is a unique ABC family member, as all other ABC transporters function as active pumps, moving biomolecules against their concentration gradients.
source: CFTR is a unique family member, as all other ABC transporters function as active pumps, moving biomolecules against their concentration gradients
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR's unique function among ABC transporters, supported by citations.

claim: The domain organization of CFTR comprises two transmembrane domains (TMDs) and two cytosolic NBDs.
source: The domain organization of CFTR is similar to that of canonical ABC transporters, comprising two transmembrane domains (TMDs) and two cytosolic NBDs.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about CFTR.

claim: A unique feature of CFTR is the regulatory domain (R) which contains multiple phosphorylation sites and connects the two NBDs.
source: A unique feature of CFTR is the regulatory domain (R) which contains multiple phosphorylation sites and connects the two NBDs
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about CFTR's unique regulatory domain.

claim: In the resting (non-conducting) state, the funnel-shaped pore is inward-facing and is solvent accessible only to the cytoplasm.
source: In the resting (non-conducting) state, the funnel-shaped pore is inward-facing and is solvent accessible only to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited (Liu et al., 2017b; Zhang and Chen, 2016).

claim: In the resting state, the NBDs are separated, and the R domain is wedged between them, preventing their dimerization.
source: The NBDs are separated, and the R domain is wedged between them, preventing their dimerization (Liu et al., 2017b; Zhang and Chen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited.

claim: Upon phosphorylation of the R domain by PKA, it disengages from its inhibitory position and shifts aside.
source: Upon phosphorylation of the R domain by PKA, it disengages from its inhibitory position and shifts aside (Picciotto et al., 1992; Tabcharani et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental studies.

claim: After R domain phosphorylation, the NBDs bind ATP and form a 'head-to-tail' dimer.
source: The NBDs are now free to bind ATP and form a ''head-to-tail'' dimer (Rees et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2018; Mense et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by cited structural and functional studies.

claim: In CFTR, only one of the ATP sites is hydrolysis-competent while the other (termed the degenerate site) can only bind ATP but not hydrolyze it.
source: In CFTR, like in some other ABC transporters, only one of the ATP sites is hydrolysis-competent while the other (termed the degenerate site) can only bind ATP but not hydrolyze it (Hohl et al., 2012; Csanády et al., 2019; Stockner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: Formation of the NBDs dimer leads to rearrangements of transmembrane gating residues and subsequent channel opening.
source: Formation of the NBDs dimer leads to rearrangements of transmembrane gating residues and subsequent channel opening.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR gating mechanism.

claim: Hydrolysis of ATP at the catalytic site and release of hydrolysis products leads to opening of the NBDs, channel closure, and resetting of the system.
source: Hydrolysis of ATP at the catalytic site and release of hydrolysis products leads to opening of the NBDs, channel closure, and resetting of the system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR gating cycle.

claim: Most proteins and enzymes are allosteric, where ligand binding at one site affects the functional properties of another (often distant) site.
source: It is now broadly recognized that most proteins and enzymes are allosteric, where ligand binding at one site affects the functional properties of another (often distant) site
evidence: This is established knowledge in protein science, supported by multiple citations.

claim: According to the KNF model, the protein exists in a single conformation (an inactive one) to which the allosteric ligand binds, inducing a conformational change that leads to the active conformation.
source: According to Koshland, Némethy, and Filmer (KNF model, Koshland et al., 1966), the protein exists in a single conformation (an inactive one) to which the allosteric ligand binds, inducing a conformational change that leads to the active conformation.
evidence: This is a description of the classical KNF model, cited from Koshland et al., 1966.

claim: According to the MWC model, proteins pre-exist in multiple conformations, and the allosteric ligand preferentially binds to the active conformer, leading to a redistribution of the conformational distributions toward the active one.
source: Monod, Wyman, and Changeux (MWC model, Monod et al., 1965) introduced the concept of 'conformational selection', according to which proteins pre-exist in multiple conformation, and the allosteric ligand preferentially binds to the active conformer, leading to a redistribution of the conformational distributions toward the active one
evidence: This is a description of the classical MWC model, cited from Monod et al., 1965.

claim: An alternative allosteric mechanism termed 'dynamic mechanism' exists, where allostery is mediated by changes in dynamic fluctuations around a mean conformation in the absence of a noticeable conformational change.
source: More recently, an alternative allosteric mechanism was demonstrated, termed 'dynamic mechanism' (Motlagh et al., 2014; Nussinov and Tsai, 2015), where allostery is mediated by changes in dynamic fluctuations around a mean conformation in the absence of a noticeable conformational change
evidence: This is cited from recent literature on allosteric mechanisms.

claim: Long-range allosteric communications are essential to the function of CFTR.
source: There are abundant examples that long-range allosteric communications are essential to the function of CFTR.
evidence: This is supported by multiple examples and citations provided in the manuscript.

claim: In CFTR, the binding site of ATP and the affected gating residues are separated by 60–70 Å.
source: where the binding site of the effector molecule (ATP) and the affected gating residues are separated by 60–70 Å (Liu et al., 2017b; Zhang et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by structural studies cited.

claim: ATP-dependent dimerization of the NBDs is insufficient for channel opening which additionally depends on an allosteric pathway that connects the NBDs and the channel pore.
source: Levring et al. demonstrated that ATP-dependent dimerization of the NBDs is insufficient for channel opening which additionally depends on an allosteric pathway that connects the NBDs and the channel pore (Levring et al., 2023)
evidence: This is cited from Levring et al., 2023.

claim: The allosteric signal in CFTR originates at the NBDs and gradually propagates toward the gating residues along a clear longitudinal protein axis.
source: Sorum et al. reached similar conclusions, and suggested that this allosteric signal originates at the NBDs and gradually propagates toward the gating residues along a clear longitudinal protein axis (Sorum et al., 2015)
evidence: This is cited from Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: Point mutations at the cytosolic loops increase channel open probability (even in the absence of ATP) by shifting a pre-existing conformational equilibrium toward the ligand bound conducting conformation.
source: point mutations at the cytosolic loops increase channel open probability (even in the absence of ATP) by shifting a pre-existing conformational equilibrium toward the ligand bound conducting conformation (Wang et al., 2010)
evidence: This is cited from Wang et al., 2010.

claim: The potentiator drug ivacaftor and the dual-function modulator elexacaftor do not bind in the proximity of the gating residues yet increase the open probability (Po) of the channel.
source: The potentiator drug ivacaftor and the dual-function modulator elexacaftor do not bind in the proximity of the gating residues (Liu et al., 2019; Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022a) yet increase the open probability (Po) of the channel (Eckford et al., 2012; Shaughnessy et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by cited structural and functional studies.

claim: GNM-based approaches have been very successful in describing global conformational dynamics of proteins.
source: Despite, or because of, its simplicity, GNM-based approaches have been very successful in describing global conformational dynamics of proteins (Yang and Bahar, 2005; Li et al., 2014; Acar et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on GNM applications.

claim: GNM-TE identified 60 residues as the main allosteric sources in dephosphorylated ATP-free CFTR.
source: GNM-TE identified 60 residues (out of 1480) that are the main allosteric sources (i.e. allosteric peaks) in dephosphorylated ATP-free CFTR (Figure 1)
evidence: This is a direct result from the GNM-TE computational analysis presented in the study.

claim: Of the 60 residues that serve as main allosteric sources, 22 were located within 4 Å of a hinge residue, and this co-localization was highly statistically significant.
source: Of the 60 residues that serve as main allosteric sources, 22 were located within 4 Å of a hinge residue, and this co-localization was highly statistically significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the computational results.

claim: The GNM-TE-based identification of functionally essential residues has a mean value of 8 correct guesses compared to 0.7 for random allocation (p=9×e–13).
source: the random allocation has a mean value of 0.7 correct guesses while the GNM-TE-based identification has a mean value of 8 (p=9×e–13)
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing GNM-TE predictions with random allocation.

claim: Despite the structural similarity between the two NBDs, a clear asymmetry can be observed between them, with NBD2 which harbors the catalytic Walker B glutamate providing the higher allosteric signaling.
source: despite the structural similarity between the two NBDs, a clear asymmetry can be observed between them, with NBD2 which harbors the catalytic Walker B glutamate providing the higher allosteric signaling (Figures 1 and 2A)
evidence: This is observed from the GNM-TE analysis results shown in the figures.

claim: In ATP-free CFTR, the entropy sources residues are found predominantly on the NBDs and are largely absent from the TMDs.
source: the entropy sources residues (i.e. residues that drive allostery) are found predominantly on the NBDs and are largely absent from the TMDs
evidence: This is observed from the GNM-TE analysis results shown in Figures 1 and 2A.

claim: The only TMD residues that serve as entropic sources in ATP-free CFTR are those found at or near intracellular loops 2 and 3.
source: The only TMD residues that serve as entropic sources are those found at or near intracellular loops 2 and 3 (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is observed from the GNM-TE analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Even when the NBDs are completely separated and the composite ATP-binding sites are yet to form, the dynamic infrastructure for nucleotide binding is already present, poised for binding of the ligand.
source: This demonstrates that even when the NBDs are completely separated and the composite ATP-binding sites are yet to form, the dynamic infrastructure for nucleotide binding is already present, poised for binding of the ligand.
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE analysis of ATP-free CFTR showing allosteric peaks near ATP-binding sites.

claim: In the ATP-free state, some of the main entropy peaks located in the NBDs are slightly shifted from the ATP-binding residues and correspond to adjacent residues.
source: some of the main entropy peaks (i.e. entropy sources) located in the NBDs are slightly shifted from the ATP-binding residues (Figure 1) and correspond to adjacent residues
evidence: This is observed from the GNM-TE analysis results shown in Figure 1.

claim: The entropy peak shift disappears once ATP is bound, and the entropy source role is transferred from the neighboring residues to the ATP-binding residues themselves.
source: This shift disappears once ATP is bound, and the entropy source role is transferred from the neighboring residues to the ATP-binding residues themselves
evidence: This is observed by comparing GNM-TE results between ATP-free and ATP-bound states.

claim: Upon removal of the slowest GNM mode, a new cluster of residues that serve as allosteric sources was revealed, distributed roughly symmetrically in the TMDs and including the putative gating residues.
source: Upon removal of the slowest GNM mode, a new cluster of residues that serve as allosteric sources was revealed (Figure 2B). These residues, which are distributed roughly symmetrically in the TMDs, include the putative gating residues (e.g. P99, T338, S341, Liu et al., 2017b)
evidence: This is observed from GNM-TE analysis after removing the slowest mode, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The residues that form the ivacaftor binding site were revealed as entropy sources by removal of the slowest GNM mode.
source: The residues that form the ivacaftor binding site (Liu et al., 2019) were also revealed as entropy sources by removal of the slowest GNM mode (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is observed from GNM-TE analysis after removing the slowest mode, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Removal of the second slowest GNM mode reveals a highly asymmetric cluster of TMD residues comprised solely of residues in TMD1, located at and just above the future site for docking of the regulatory domain.
source: Removal of the next slowest GNM mode reveals another cluster of TMD residues that serve as entropy/allostery sources. Unlike the above-described symmetric cluster, this cluster is highly asymmetric, and is comprised solely of residues in TMD1 (Figure 2C). Interestingly, this cluster of residues is located at and just above the future site for docking of the regulatory domain
evidence: This is observed from GNM-TE analysis after removing the two slowest modes, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Phosphorylation and binding of ATP greatly rewires the overall allosteric connectivity in CFTR.
source: We observed that phosphorylation and binding of ATP greatly rewires the overall allosteric connectivity in CFTR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and compare Figures 1 and 3A)
evidence: This is observed by comparing GNM-TE results between ATP-free and ATP-bound states.

claim: Phosphorylation and binding of ATP focuses the dynamics of CFTR, which pre-existed in a more diffuse manner in the unphosphorylated ATP-free state.
source: This suggests that phosphorylation and binding of ATP focuses the dynamics of CFTR, which pre-existed in a more diffuse manner in the unphosphorylated ATP-free state.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the sharpness of entropy peaks between ATP-free and ATP-bound states.

claim: Upon binding of ATP, the entropy peaks in the NBDs closely match the location of the ATP-binding residues.
source: This offset largely disappears upon binding of ATP, and the entropy peaks in the NBDs now closely match the location of the ATP-binding residues (compare Figures 1 and 3A)
evidence: This is observed by comparing GNM-TE results shown in Figures 1 and 3A.

claim: Upon phosphorylation and binding of ATP, the residues that surround the ion permeation channel serve as main entropy sources in the TMDs.
source: In the TMDs, the residues that serve as main entropy sources are those that surround the ion permeation channel (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is observed from GNM-TE analysis of ATP-bound CFTR shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Upon phosphorylation and binding of ATP, the gating and pore lining residues assume a more dominant role in allosteric signaling.
source: This means that upon phosphorylation and binding of ATP the gating and pore lining residues assume a more dominant role in allosteric signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing GNM-TE results between ATP-free and ATP-bound states.

claim: Binding of ATP had a very similar effect in both human and zebrafish CFTR homologues, suggesting that the allosteric effects of ATP binding are robust and conserved.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, binding of ATP had a very similar effect in both CFTR homologues, suggesting that the allosteric effects of ATP binding are robust and conserved.
evidence: This is observed by comparing GNM-TE results for human and zebrafish CFTR.

claim: In the phosphorylated ATP-bound state, after removing the two slowest modes, the entropy sources in the NBDs have migrated from the ATP-binding sites at the dimer interface toward the intracellular loops.
source: First, the entropy sources in the NBDs have now migrated from the ATP-binding sites at the dimer interface toward the intracellular loops, perfectly positioned to transmit the signal to the TMDs.
evidence: This is observed from GNM-TE analysis after removing the two slowest modes, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the phosphorylated ATP-bound state, after removing the two slowest modes, the TMD allosteric peaks surrounding the gating residues and the ion permeation pathway have migrated toward the extracellular exit.
source: Second, the TMD allosteric peaks surrounding the gating residues and the ion permeation pathway have migrated toward the extracellular exit, as if to prepare for ion exit.
evidence: This is observed from GNM-TE analysis after removing the two slowest modes, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A cluster of residues that serve as strong entropy sources appeared in TMD1 exclusively, comprising or adjacent to the site of interaction of the regulatory (R) domain.
source: Lastly, a cluster of residues that serve as strong entropy sources appeared in the TMDs in an asymmetric manner (Figure 3C–D). These residues are found exclusively in TMD1 and comprise or are adjacent to the site of interaction of the regulatory (R) domain
evidence: This is observed from GNM-TE analysis after removing the two slowest modes, shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The presence of a cluster of information-transmitting residues in the vicinity of the docking site of the R domain may explain previous observations that deletion of the R domain leads to fewer channel opening events.
source: The presence of this cluster of information-transmitting residues in the vicinity of the docking site of the R domain may explain previous observations that deletion of the R domain leads to fewer channel opening events
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE results and cited experimental observations from Winter and Welsh, 1997; Ma et al., 1997.

claim: The 2D cross-correlation map is dominated by large and continuous patches of red (positive correlation) and blue (negative correlation) areas, suggesting that global rigid body motions with a relatively small number of hinges underlie the conformational change.
source: The map is dominated by large and continuous patches of red (positive correlation) and blue (negative correlation) areas... These observations suggest that, as inferred from the cryo-EM structures of CFTR (Liu et al., 2017b; Zhang et al., 2018), global rigid body motions with a relatively small number of hinges underlie this conformational change
evidence: This is inferred from the ANM-LD cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The conformational changes of CFTR are similar to those of canonical ABC exporters.
source: the conformational changes of CFTR are similar to those of canonical ABC exporters
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the cross-correlation map of CFTR with that of PglK, a canonical ABC exporter.

claim: The two NBDs display asymmetric allosteric connectivity: NBD1 shows a tighter correlation with the residues that surround the permeation pathway.
source: The two NBDs display asymmetric allosteric connectivity: NBD1 shows a tighter correlation with the residues that surround the permeation pathway (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is observed from the ANM-LD cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: NBD2 is more strongly correlated with ECL1 (extracellular loop 1) which is known to stabilize the conducting state of the channel.
source: while NBD2 (harboring the catalytic Walker B glutamate) is more strongly correlated with ECL1 (extracellular loop 1) (Figure 4C) which is known to stabilize the conducting state of the channel (Infield et al., 2016)
evidence: This is observed from the ANM-LD cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C, with supporting citation.

claim: The conformational change from the dephosphorylated ATP-free state to the phosphorylated ATP-bound one begins with the movement of the NBDs.
source: in parallel simulations we repeatedly observed that the conformational change from the dephosphorylated ATP-free state to the phosphorylated ATP-bound one begins with the movement of the NBDs
evidence: This is observed from repeated ANM-LD simulations.

claim: The movement of NBD2 is the leading event and those of ICL2/3, TMD2/TM8, and ECL1 follow, and the allosteric signal propagates from NBD2 to ICL2/3, TMD2/TM8, and ECL1.
source: This observation strongly suggests that the movement of NBD2 is the leading event and those of ICL2/3, TMD2/TM8, and ECL1 follow, and that the allosteric signal propagates from NBD2 to ICL2/3, TMD2/TM8, and ECL1 (Figure 5 center, green arrows)
evidence: This is inferred from time-delayed cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: From ECL1 the allosteric signal propagates to NBD1.
source: From ECL1 the allosteric signal propagates to NBD1: The movements of these two domains are highly correlated, but only if ECL1 leads and NBD1 follows (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 magenta rectangles, Figure 5 step II, and Figure 5 center, magenta arrow)
evidence: This is inferred from time-delayed cross-correlation analysis.

claim: From NBD1 the allosteric signal propagates to the gating residues and to the TM helices that surround the permeation pathway.
source: from NBD1 the allosteric signal propagates to the gating residues and to the TM helices that surround the permeation pathway: The movements of these domains are only synchronized if the former leads and the latter follows
evidence: This is inferred from time-delayed cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The allosteric signal propagates from the permeation pathway to NBD2, thus completing the cycle of allosteric transduction.
source: We therefore conclude that the allosteric signal propagates from the permeation pathway to NBD2, thus completing the cycle of allosteric transduction (Figure 5 center, orange arrow)
evidence: This is inferred from time-delayed cross-correlation analysis.

claim: There are currently four FDA-approved drugs that are used to treat CF: lumacaftor (VX-809), tezacaftor (VX-661), ivacaftor (VX-770), and elexacaftor (VX-445).
source: There are currently four FDA-approved drugs that are used to treat CF: The type I correctors lumacaftor (VX-809) and tezacaftor (VX-661)... The potentiator ivacaftor (VX-770)... and the dual-function type III corrector elexacaftor (VX-445)
evidence: This is established knowledge about FDA-approved CF drugs.

claim: The type I correctors lumacaftor and tezacaftor stabilize mutant CFTR variants, reducing premature protein degradation and improving surface presentation of the mature channel.
source: The type I correctors lumacaftor (VX-809) and tezacaftor (VX-661) stabilize mutant CFTR variants (predominantly the most common ΔF508 mutation) reducing premature protein degradation and improving surface presentation of the mature channel
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of type I correctors, supported by citations.

claim: The potentiator ivacaftor enhances the activity of conductance-defective mutants by increasing the open probability (Po) of the channel.
source: The potentiator ivacaftor (VX-770) enhances the activity of conductance-defective mutants by increasing the open probability (Po) of the channel
evidence: This is established knowledge about ivacaftor's mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The dual-function type III corrector elexacaftor stabilizes unstable variants and increases channel open probability.
source: the dual-function type III corrector elexacaftor (VX-445) stabilizes unstable variants and increases channel open probability
evidence: This is established knowledge about elexacaftor's mechanism, supported by citations.

claim: The type I correctors lumacaftor and tezacaftor bind at 'valleys', i.e., to residues that are not allosteric sources.
source: the type I correctors lumacaftor and tezacaftor bind at 'valleys', i.e., to residues that are not allosteric sources
evidence: This is observed from GNM-TE analysis of drug-bound CFTR shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The mechanism of type I correctors (lumacaftor and tezacaftor) is to improve the function of CFTR by lowering its ∆G(folding) rather than by modulating its activity.
source: These results are consistent with the mechanism of these drugs which improve the function of CFTR by lowering its ∆G(folding) rather than by modulating its activity (Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022b)
evidence: This is cited from Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022b and is consistent with the GNM-TE results.

claim: The residues that comprise the binding sites for ivacaftor and elexacaftor include ones that serve as main allosteric sources.
source: the residues that comprise the binding sites for ivacaftor and elexacaftor also include ones that serve as main allosteric sources (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is observed from GNM-TE analysis of drug-bound CFTR shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The ivacaftor docking site and the ATP-binding site send information to a very similar set of residues (Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.83).
source: As shown in Figure 6C, the two profiles showed remarkable overlap: The ivacaftor docking site and the ATP-binding site send information to a very similar set of residues (Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.83)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from GNM-TE analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ivacaftor increases the opening probability not by directly affecting the gating residues but rather indirectly by mimicking the allosteric signaling evoked by ATP binding.
source: These observations suggest that ivacaftor increases the opening probability not by directly affecting the gating residues but rather indirectly by mimicking the allosteric signaling evoked by ATP binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE analysis showing similar information transfer patterns between ivacaftor and ATP binding sites.

claim: Ivacaftor exerts its potentiating effect by mimicking the combined allosteric output of the ATP-binding and gating residues, compensating for any potential allosteric transduction short circuit caused by mutations.
source: This result suggests that ivacaftor exerts its potentiating effect by mimicking the combined allosteric output of the ATP-binding and gating residues, compensating for any potential allosteric transduction short circuit caused by mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the allosteric signaling patterns shown in Figure 6B-F.

claim: In the absence of phosphorylation and ATP, CFTR adopts solely the NBDs-open conformation and spontaneous conversions to the NBDs-closed conformation are not seen.
source: In the absence of phosphorylation and ATP, CFTR adopts solely the NBDs-open conformation and spontaneous conversions to the NBDs-closed conformation are not seen (Levring et al., 2023)
evidence: This is cited from Levring et al., 2023.

claim: Multiple phosphorylation events are required to dislodge the R domain from its obstructing position, presenting a very large energetic barrier.
source: multiple phosphorylation events are required to dislodge the R domain from its obstructing position, presenting a very large energetic barrier (Liu et al., 2017b; Gadsby and Nairn, 1999)
evidence: This is cited from Liu et al., 2017b and Gadsby and Nairn, 1999.

claim: The first step of the conformational change, movement of the R domain, occurs by an induced fit mechanism, where the reversible covalent phosphorylation is the allosteric ligand.
source: we currently propose that this step occurs by an induced fit mechanism, where the reversible covalent phosphorylation is the allosteric ligand (Figure 7, step I)
evidence: This is proposed based on the conformational homogeneity of dephosphorylated ATP-free CFTR and the large energetic barrier for R domain movement.

claim: Single molecule studies showed that even after phosphorylation the NBDs solely adopt the open conformation and do not spontaneously close unless ATP is added.
source: single molecule studies showed that even after phosphorylation the NBDs solely adopt the open conformation and do not spontaneously close unless ATP is added
evidence: This is cited from Levring et al., 2023.

claim: Once ATP was added, all the molecules converted to the closed-NBD conformation and were never seen to spontaneously open their NBDs.
